items.note: Broman & Woo: how to keep the spreadsheet itself sane, before R ever sees it. Change one habit from this.

stages.title: Your first plot and test
can: I can plot my own measurements with every replicate showing
I can run the test that suits my design and read the output
I can save a figure at a size and resolution a journal accepts

items.title: Data Analysis and Visualisation in R for Ecologists (Data Carpentry)
items.note: Real messy data, plotted and summarised. Nothing to do with ecology, really.

items.title: ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis
items.note: Free. How the plotting grammar fits together, so you stop copying examples.

items.title: Learning Statistics with R
items.note: Free, long, and kind: statistics and R taught together, assuming neither.

stages.title: One analysis, from file to figure
can: One script takes my raw file and makes the figure, with nothing done by hand

items.title: Quarto: get started
items.note: Put the text, the code and the figures in one document that rebuilds itself. This is what makes it reproducible.

items.title: TidyTuesday
items.note: A new dataset every week, and hundreds of people's scripts for it. The best way to see how others do it.

stages.title: Use it in your own work

protocols.goal: choosing and running the right test
protocols.title: Statistics for experiments: which test, and why
protocols.summary: t-test, ANOVA and their assumptions, in the words of an experiment: replicates, controls, and what a p-value does and does not tell you.

stages.title: What your numbers are
can: I can say what my unit of analysis is for a given experiment
I know the difference between a technical and a biological replicate
I can describe my data before testing it: mean, spread, and a plot

items.title: Points of Significance (Nature Methods)
items.note: Two-page columns, free, each on one idea: error bars, replication, significance. Start here and read them in order.

items.title: Introduction to Modern Statistics
items.note: Free, clear, and full of real data. The textbook if you want one.

items.title: StatQuest
items.note: Short videos that explain one test at a time, drawn out slowly. Many bench scientists learn this way.

stages.title: Choosing the test
can: I can pick between a t-test, a paired t-test and ANOVA for my design
I can state the assumptions of the test I chose
I know what to do about multiple comparisons

items.title: Handbook of Biological Statistics
items.note: McDonald's free handbook: for each test, when to use it, how, and what to report. The most practical thing on this list.

items.title: The ASA statement on p-values
items.note: Six short principles from the American Statistical Association. Two pages that change how you write results.

items.title: Scientists rise up against statistical significance
items.note: Why 'not significant' doesn't mean 'no effect'. Free, and short.

stages.title: Running it, and reporting it
can: I can run my test in R or GraphPad and read every number it gives back
I report effect size and uncertainty, not only a p-value
I can work out a sample size before the experiment, not after

items.title: Learning Statistics with R
items.note: Free. Does the test in R next to the explanation, which is the fastest way to trust the output.

items.title: G*Power
items.note: Free software for sample size and power. Use it before you start, even roughly.

items.title: Beyond bar and line graphs
items.note: Plot the data, not a summary of it. The figure change that makes the statistics honest.

stages.title: Reanalyse one of your own experiments
can: I've redone the statistics of one finished experiment, and can defend every choice

items.title: Nested analyses of cell-based data (SuperPlots)
items.note: A worked example of the mistake almost everyone makes with replicates, and how to fix the plot and the test together.

stages.title: Use it in your own work

protocols.title: Figures your reviewers won't ask you to redo
protocols.summary: One script that makes the figure, so it can be remade when the data changes: axes, colour, honesty, and the file the journal actually wants.

stages.title: What makes a figure readable
can: I can choose the plot type that suits my data, not the one I always use
I can label axes with units so no caption is needed to read them
I can tell when my figure is hiding the data

items.title: Fundamentals of Data Visualization
items.note: Free. Each chapter shows a bad figure and the better one, with the reason.

items.title: Ten Simple Rules for Better Figures
items.note: Ten rules, two pages, open access. The fastest improvement available to anyone.

items.title: Points of View (Nature Methods)
items.note: The visualisation companion to Points of Significance: colour, salience and layout, one page each.

stages.title: Colour, and who can read it
can: I use a palette that survives colour blindness and a black-and-white printer
I never use a rainbow scale for continuous data, and can say why
My colours mean the same thing in every panel

items.title: ColorBrewer
items.note: Palettes chosen for maps and plots, with colour-blind and print-safe filters.

items.title: The misuse of colour in science communication
items.note: Why jet and rainbow scales mislead, with the alternatives. Open access.

items.title: viridis
items.note: The default good answer for continuous colour, in R and Python alike.

stages.title: The figure, from a script
can: My figure is made by a script I can rerun when the data changes
I can build a multi-panel figure with consistent sizes and fonts
I can export at the width, font size and format the journal asks for

items.title: ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis
items.note: Free. The R side, including arranging panels and saving at an exact size.

items.title: Matplotlib tutorials
items.note: The Python side, from the project itself.

items.title: The R Graph Gallery
items.note: Hundreds of plots with their code. Find the one you want and take the code.

stages.title: Remake one of your own figures
can: One of my published or submitted figures now comes out of a script, identical

items.title: Quarto: get started
items.note: Text, code and figures in one document that rebuilds itself. Then a data fix never means redrawing by hand.
